answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the same resource type used for Cosmos DB accounts exposing MongoDB endpoints).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName='eastus' --default-consistency-level Session. MongoDB-specific flags live under az cosmosdb and az cosmosdb mongodb subcommands. This is in the core az CLI (no extra extension required).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (apiVersion e.g. 2021-04-15 or newer). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account. Use these to declare the account and then create MongoDB databases/collections via azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection (or the provider's Mongo resources).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical connection string (standard Mongo driver): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. SRV form (if supported): mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port commonly 10255 when using non-SRV endpoints; TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true) and replicaSet=globaldb is usually required for Cosmos Mongo compatibility, plus retryWrites often disabled.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure-managed MongoDB-compatible clusters are typically billed either by provisioned throughput/RUs (classic Cosmos DB Mongo API) or by vCore-based instance sizes for managed MongoDB clusters (e.g. compute tiers named like M30, billed by vCores + storage). For a cluster described as M30 you should expect vCore-based billing (compute tier + storage), not RU-based billing. Some SKUs may also offer a serverless option, but if you see M30 the cluster is vCore-based.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary authentication is MongoDB native auth (SCRAM username/password) and X.509 client cert auth where supported. For Azure-managed MongoDB compatibility, Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is generally not supported in the same way it is for Azure SQL/Cosmos SQL APIs — drivers normally authenticate with the Mongo user credentials provisioned on the account. There is no standard MongoDB driver flow that exchanges an Azure AD token directly with the service in most managed MongoDB-compatible Azure offerings.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the platform's official MongoDB driver (for Node.js use the mongodb npm package). There is no separate DocumentDB/MongoDB-specific client SDK required: standard MongoDB drivers work against the managed endpoint. (For other Azure APIs you can use Azure SDKs, but for Mongo API use Mongo drivers.)

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector indexes on a Mongo-compatible cluster use the MongoDB 7-style vector index declarations. Example (approximate syntax): db.touchpoints.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vec_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', metric: 'cosine' } } ). Other algorithms you might see are 'hnsw', 'ivf', and a DiskANN option on the service; exact option names vary by provider. Use createIndex on the collection with a field mapped as type 'vector' and algorithm options in the index options object.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is done by integrating with a search service rather than via Mongo queries on the managed endpoint: use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) and index the MongoDB data (via change feed or an indexer) to perform full-text or hybrid vector+text search. Alternatively, if the managed offering supports built-in vector search, combine vector indexes with a text index in the app side or use an external search engine for hybrid relevance blending.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Newer managed clusters advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol support (so drivers targeting 7.x should work). Historically many Azure Mongo-compatible offerings lagged upstream and omitted or limited features such as server-side JavaScript execution (db.eval/$where), some admin commands, and certain change-data-capture internals. Expect omissions around server-side JS, direct file system access, and some low-level admin commands. Verify the exact supported server version from the account's advertised compatibility level.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no official Azure DocumentDB/Mongo emulator that fully replicates the managed cluster features. For local development run a local MongoDB docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) on the default Mongo port 27017. Note: local Mongo will not emulate provider-specific features (vector indexes, DiskANN, provider-specific admin behaviors).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported on MongoDB 3.6+ wire protocol when the managed cluster implements them. If the managed cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0, change streams should be available via the driver watch() API. No special flag beyond using a replica-set/sharded deployment that supports change streams is normally required, but some managed offerings historically disabled or limited change streams — verify by calling watch() or checking provider docs.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile (named documentdb) to get the service-specific data-plane tools and inspectors. The general Azure MCP server covers resource management but the documentdb MCP server provides Mongo-aware tools (index viewers, explain plan inspectors).

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (the 'Core (SQL)' API was originally called DocumentDB). The MongoDB-compatible offering is usually exposed as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB API' or 'Azure managed MongoDB' depending on the SKU. The open-source DocumentDB project is unrelated. In short: Azure DocumentDB (old name) -> Azure Cosmos DB; the Mongo API is a compatibility layer or separate managed Mongo offering depending on SKU.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: For a MongoDB-compatible endpoint you should treat it as a Mongo server from the application's perspective and use standard MongoDB drivers. Under the hood the provider may be running the upstream MongoDB server or a translation layer (e.g. Cosmos translation). Either way, client code uses the MongoDB driver and typical connection strings; you must, however, be cautious about provider-specific limitations (unsupported admin commands, server-side scripting, or different index/aggregation behaviour).

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field. Example approximate command: db.touchpoints.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'embedding_vec_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine' }}) — tune dimensions and algorithm to match the model and cluster capabilities.

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will the sample use to reconstruct a customer's journey (grouping and sorting)?
answers.answer: Use a pipeline that filters by customerId, sorts by timestamp, groups to collect an ordered array of events, and projects a timeline. Example pipeline steps: [ { $match: { customerId: '<id>' } }, { $sort: { timestamp: 1 } }, { $group: { _id: '$customerId', events: { $push: { channel: '$channel', ts: '$timestamp', type: '$type', metadata: '$metadata' } } } }, { $project: { _id:0, customerId:'$_id', timeline:'$events' } } ].

answers.question: Which database should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_04 for all collections and indexes created by the sample.

answers.question: How should the Node.js sample connect to the cluster at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to the official mongodb driver (mongodb npm package). Do not persist credentials in files; provide a .env.example with a placeholder.

answers.question: What client operation does the sample use to fetch changes or drive hybrid search/indexing?
answers.answer: Use the MongoDB change stream API (collection.watch()) to stream touchpoint changes for downstream indexing to Azure Cognitive Search or to update vector indexes. If change streams are not available, fall back to a timestamp-based incremental poll using a lastSeen timestamp query on the timestamp field.
